# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I want to talk about doorways.

Not metaphorically—though they certainly work that way in literature and life, serving as thresholds between one state and another, representing change and passage and new beginnings. I've read those essays. I understand the symbolism. But I want to talk about actual doorways, the physical wooden or metal frames that separate interior from exterior, private from public, one room from another. I want to talk about them because I've been noticing them lately, really noticing them, and it strikes me as odd that we don't spend more time thinking about how remarkable they are.

Consider what a doorway is, functionally. It's a deliberate gap in a barrier. That's interesting enough on its own. Humans erected walls, and then we immediately had to create holes in those walls because walls, while useful for keeping out weather and intruders, are not useful for letting people move through spaces. So we invented doors, which are movable walls, ways to seal or unseal the opening. The whole system is one of negotiation—how to be separate and connected simultaneously.

But the thing about doorways, especially old ones, is the craftsmanship. I was in a house built in 1887 recently, and I found myself just looking at the door frame for an embarrassingly long time. The wood had been carefully cut, fitted together at precise angles, built to last. The proportions seemed to follow some rule I couldn't quite articulate—the height relative to the width, the thickness of the frame itself. There was a plane of wood, maybe an eighth of an inch thick, that beveled inward, creating a subtle shadow line. Why had someone bothered? No one would notice. Or rather, thousands of people would pass through that doorway and none of them would consciously notice, but they would feel it. The doorway would feel right, would have grace, without their knowing why.

This is what strikes me about ordinary things—that so much care was lavished on them, continues to be lavished on them, largely unobserved.

We live in an age of efficiency, where I think we've sometimes confused the purpose of things with the only acceptable way to make them. A doorway needs to connect two spaces. That's its functional requirement. You could accomplish that with a hole in the wall. But humans have, across cultures and centuries, decided that a doorway should also be beautiful, or at least should possess a certain rightness of proportion. Someone had to decide on those proportions. Someone had to care enough to decide.

I find this oddly moving.

There's something defiant about it, too, something that suggests values operating underneath our utilitarian surface. We could build everything cheaply, quickly, with no regard for anything beyond function. We could, and often do. But some people don't. Some people will spend extra time and money and mental energy making a doorway that doesn't need to be beautiful but will be anyway. It will be beautiful because someone believes that things matter even when no one is watching, even when no one will notice, even when the only reward is an internal knowledge that you did something well.

I think about this in relation to writing, to the work of finding exactly the right word, the right rhythm, the right image. Why does it matter? The reader will get the general sense without perfect precision. Surely the difference between a good sentence and a great sentence is negligible in terms of outcome. You're telling yourself a story either way. You're receiving the information.

But it matters in a way I can't quite explain but feel absolutely. It matters the way that doorway frame matters, with its beveled edge creating a shadow line that you'll never consciously register but will make the entire room feel more thoughtfully designed.

This is connected to something I've been thinking about regarding attention and meaning. We are starved for attention in our culture. Everyone wants ours, and everyone is starving to receive it. We rush. We speed-consume. We extract information and move on. I do this constantly. I'll read a news article, scroll through writing, consume and discard. There's an argument that this is inevitable, that no one has time to sit and contemplate doorways, and I understand that argument. But I also wonder if some of our anxiety and dissatisfaction comes from this very fact—that we are always being asked to consume quickly, to not think too carefully, to accept the bare minimum because we don't have time for anything more.

What if we didn't? What if we took time to notice the beveled edge of a doorway? Not even to think about it deeply, just to see it. To register that someone cared about that shadow line.

There's something about this that strikes at some deep human need. I was in a pottery workshop once, watching someone throw a bowl on a wheel, and the instructor said something that stuck with me. She said that making something by hand teaches you something about the world that you can't learn any other way. You learn friction. You learn resistance. You learn the actual limitations of material. And you learn that care is physical. It's not an abstract virtue. It's the pressure you apply with your thumb, the steadiness of your hand, the attention in your body.

When you use that bowl—when you hold it, fill it with water or soup or nothing but air—your hands know that someone spent hours learning to make this. Your hands remember the care even if your conscious mind doesn't.

I think about the people who cut those doorway frames in 1887. I don't know their names. They're long dead. No one is visiting that house thinking "thank goodness these craftsmen existed." But the house is better because they did. It's more pleasant to move through. It has a dignity that cheaper, faster construction wouldn't have provided.

There's also something about skill and mastery that matters here. The ability to cut a precise angle, to fit pieces together so they stay together, to proportion something aesthetically—these are skills that take time to develop. They require attention. They require effort. In a world that increasingly rewards speed and efficiency, there's something almost radical about spending the time necessary to develop genuine skill, to do something well enough that it will last a century and a half and still feel right.

I'm not saying everything needs to be handcrafted. That's not practical and never was. But I'm saying there's a spectrum, and I think we've allowed ourselves to slide too far toward one end of it, convinced that all that matters is function and cost.

I was at a coffee shop recently where the barista really cared about making the coffee. Not in a performative way, though there was some of that. But in a genuine way. They ground the beans fresh, took the time to dial in the machine, poured the milk with attention. The coffee tasted noticeably better than the same coffee made quickly elsewhere. And I found myself grateful, not just for the coffee, but for the care itself. For the fact that someone had decided that how they did this work mattered.

This is available to any of us, in any work. Whether you're cutting doorframes or pouring coffee or writing sentences or doing any of the million other things that humans do, there's a choice about whether you'll do it with care or without it. Whether you'll notice the shadow line or ignore it.

I think about this a lot when I'm doing something tedious or frustrating—something that no one will really notice, that doesn't really matter in the grand scheme. Washing dishes. Filing papers. Editing something probably no one will read carefully. There's a kind of surrender possible in those moments, where I can either resent the smallness of the task or I can notice that care is available, that I can pour something into this moment that costs me nothing but attention.

It doesn't always stick. More often than I'd like, I do things quickly and poorly and move on, thinking about what comes next. But every so often I manage the other thing, and there's a quality to those moments that's different. Not better, exactly, though it is that. But different. More present. Less alienated from the work itself.

This is what I think we're actually hungry for, underneath a lot of what we think we're hungry for. Not more stuff, not more speed, not more options, but this: the possibility of doing things well, of bringing ourselves fully to bear on whatever we're doing, of knowing that someone cared about making the thing we're using, and maybe, just maybe, caring in return in some small way.

The doorway reminds us of this. It's old, and it's still here, still functioning, still beautiful. Someone made it well, and the benefits of that care have accrued across generations. None of those generations had to do anything to receive that benefit. They just had to walk through the door. The care was embedded in the object itself.

I think about what that means for legacy, for impact, for how we spend our time and energy. What are we building that will still be here, still be right, still be beautiful, when we're gone? What are we pouring care into? It doesn't have to be grand. It doesn't have to be noticed. But it matters anyway.

There's something almost defiant about that. In a culture that measures everything by immediate return, by visibility, by engagement metrics, it's genuinely radical to spend time on something no one will notice, something that won't trend or go viral, something that will only be quietly, invisibly good. And yet people do this constantly. Artists make work that will be seen by thirty people. Parents pour incalculable energy into raising human beings in the background, noticed by almost no one. Craftspeople make beautiful things that function invisibly, appreciated but not celebrated.

What motivates this? I think it's something deep in human nature, something that says that things matter intrinsically, not because of their visibility. That you matter even when no one is watching. That your work is worth doing well even though the difference might be infinitesimal to anyone but you.

I want to end by returning to the doorway, because I think that's where this really lives. I'm going to walk through hundreds of doorways in my life, maybe thousands. Most of them are pretty ordinary. Some are beautiful in obvious ways—grand, elaborate, designed to impress. But the ones that get me are the ordinary ones that have been made well. The proportions that feel right. The wood that's been carefully worked. The frame that's been fitted precisely. None of it showy. None of it necessary. All of it speaking to the same thing: someone cared about this. Someone believed it mattered.

That belief is contagious. When you notice it in a doorway, you start noticing it everywhere. In the way a staircase is designed. The balance of a ceramic cup. The curve of a chair. Some human being decided that these small things deserved care, and that care changes how you move through the world.

I think we could use more of that. Less pressure to perform, to impress, to make everything count immediately and obviously. More willingness to invest care in small, invisible things. More belief that it matters to do things well even when no one is watching.

The doorway will last. Someone who lived a hundred years ago did work that I will benefit from today and will probably benefit others a hundred years in the future. That's not nothing. That's not small. That's as close to immortality as we get.

So the next time you walk through a doorway, look at it. Look at the frame. Notice whether it's been made with care. Feel the difference it makes, even if you can't quite articulate what that difference is. And then maybe, just maybe, decide that your work—whatever it is—deserves that same care. Not because anyone's watching. Not because you'll be rewarded. But because things matter, and you matter, and the work of your hands and mind matters, whether anyone notices or not.

That's what the doorway teaches us.
